item.title: 7 Lies Estrangement Tells You About Yourself
item.description:
Family Dynamics

7 Lies Estrangement Tells You About Yourself

Estrangement can convince you that you're the problem. You're not.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • The thoughts that make estranged adults feel broken usually aren't true.
  • Blaming yourself is what a child does to survive a parent who couldn't show love the way the child needed.
  • As an adult, you can learn to notice the old, harsh voice and answer it with something truer.
Sometimes the most painful part of estrangement isn't what happened—it's the story we begin telling ourselves about what it means.
Source: Samantha Barcham / ChatGPT (OpenAI)

When I became a mother, the grief of being estranged from my own hit me in a way it never had before. Loving my daughters was immediate and total. I would do anything for them, and that fierce, unconditional love raised questions I couldn't put down: Why couldn't my own mother do this for me? What was wrong with me that she didn't?

I've since spent years researching estrangement and sitting with people living through it—mothers and fathers, sons and daughters, people who left and people who were left. And I heard the same hushed sentences again and again. Not the ones people say out loud, like, "Shouldn't I be over this by now?" but the ones they only say to themselves at two in the morning and never repeat to anyone.

These thoughts feel like private evidence that something is broken in you. They're not. They're the lies estrangement whispers when you're wired to love someone who couldn't love you back safely.

Here are the ones I hear most, and something truer you can put in their place.

1. "What was wrong with me that they couldn't love me?"

This thought usually starts early. A small child can't make sense of a parent who isn't there for them the way they need, so they land on the only explanation that feels survivable: It must be me. If I were different, they'd love me right. Believing you're the problem is easier than facing the truth—that you were small, and they were the grown-up who fell short. That's not clear thinking. It's a frightened kid doing their best.

A truer thought: There was nothing wrong with me. Something was wrong with how I was treated.

That puts the responsibility where it belongs. There isn't a flaw in you waiting to be discovered.

2. "Why do I still miss them after everything?"

This is the question that makes people feel most broken, and it has the most reassuring answer: You're not missing the harm. You're missing the person you were wired from birth to need. We're biologically built to attach to the people who raise us, and that wiring doesn't switch off because they let you down, or because you chose to step back. Missing them is a reflection of the oldest part of you still doing its job.

A truer thought: Of course I miss them. I'm wired to.

Seeing this as biology rather than weakness takes the shame out of it.

3. "I chose this, so I don't get to be sad."

Choosing distance and grieving it aren't a contradiction. People assume a decision you made on purpose shouldn't hurt, so when the grief comes anyway, you feel like a fraud for it. But you can know something was necessary and still mourn that it had to happen. Protecting yourself was the right call. It doesn't mean you don't get to feel what it cost you.

A truer thought: I can be sure of my decision and still be sad about it.

The sadness isn't proof you were wrong but that you lost something real.

4. "Aren't parents supposed to love their kids no matter what?"

For a lot of estranged sons and daughters, this is the one that cuts deepest, whether it's about a father or a mother. We're all taught that parents love their kids unconditionally, so when yours couldn't, the only explanation that seems to fit is: It must have been me. But unconditional love is an ideal, not a guarantee. Some parents simply can't give what they don't have, for reasons that were set long before you came along.

A truer thought: Most parents love their kids. Mine couldn't show it in the ways I needed, and that was about their limits, not my worth.

5. "Everyone else has a normal family. Why can't I?"

This thought tends to show up in ordinary moments: a coworker's easy phone call home, a friend's family group chat, a holiday photo that isn't complicated. It can feel like everyone else got something you didn't. But "normal families" also hide a lot. Estrangement is far more common than people admit, because most people carry it quietly, and that silence is exactly what makes you feel alone in it.

A truer thought: I'm not the only one. I'm just one of the few who says it out loud.

Knowing you're not alone doesn't fix the loss, but it does make it less lonely. There are far more of us than you'd guess.

6. "What if I regret this when they're gone?"

This is the thought that keeps you up at night because there's no way to answer it in advance. The fear of regretting it later can pull you back toward contact that wasn't safe, telling you that anything is better than a maybe-someday. But staying in a relationship that hurt you carries its own regret, and you'd live it every single day. You already know what the relationship cost you. That counts.

A truer thought: I made this choice with what I knew and what I could handle. That's not something to regret.

It's natural to grieve the relationship you wish you could have had. But your decision was based on the relationship you actually had.

7. "A stronger person would have found a way to make it work."

Plenty of estranged adults carry some version of this lie, but it gets strength backward. Staying wasn't the strong option. You likely tried for years, absorbed more than anyone knew, and stepped back only when there was nothing left to try. Walking away from someone you're wired to want is one of the hardest things a person can do. It takes more strength than staying ever could.

A truer thought: Leaving wasn't weakness. It was the strongest thing I could do for myself.

You didn't fail to hold on. You found the courage to let go of something that was hurting you.

You Don’t Need to Believe the Lies

These negative thoughts won't disappear because you've read a better suggested sentence. They're old, and they'll come back—usually when you're tired, or on a birthday or holiday, or when someone asks an innocent question about your family.

When they reappear, recognize them for what they are. Notice the old voice, understand where it came from, and answer it with what you know now.

You're not unlovable. You're a person who needed what everyone needs, from someone who couldn't give it. And you found a way to keep going anyway.

item.title: "Feeling Old" Matters More Than Your Actual Age in Bed
item.description:
Aging

"Feeling Old" Matters More Than Your Actual Age in Bed

Research finds that subjective age may shape sexual satisfaction later in life.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling older than your actual age is linked to lower sexual satisfaction and well-being.
  • Subjective age predicts the quality of one's sex life even after accounting for physical health.
  • Older adults who feel 25 to 30 years younger than their actual age are the happiest with their lives.
  • Healthy aging is about more than biology—it's also about mindset.
Source: Nani Chavez/Unsplash

How do our sex lives change as we age? Several studies have explored this question over the years, but most have addressed it through a fairly narrow lens, focusing largely on how physical changes associated with aging affect sexual experiences.

The basic storyline to emerge from these studies is that, as we get older, our odds of developing chronic health conditions increase, and this, in turn, can negatively impact sexual frequency and satisfaction.

While certainly important, looking at biological changes alone doesn't tell the full story. Independent of our health status, psychological factors such as how old we actually feel also seem to play a big role in how older adults feel both in and out of the bedroom.

Subjective Age and Sexual Satisfaction

Consider a study published in the Journal of Sex Research that looked at data from a longitudinal survey of 1,170 American adults ages 40 and older. Participants completed two surveys about 10 years apart in which they were asked several questions about their sex lives, including how much desire they have for sex, how often they do it, and the quality of their sexual experiences. They were also asked to report their subjective age, meaning the age they feel most of the time.

Results indicated that frequency, quality, and interest in sex all declined over that 10-year period. Also, consistent with previous research, those who remained in better health tended to maintain more active and satisfying sex lives.

So how did subjective age factor into all of this? Although it was unrelated to how often people had sex, feeling older than one's actual age predicted less interest in sex over time, as well as lower levels of sexual satisfaction. Conversely, those who felt younger than they actually were had more sexual desire and were happier with their sex lives.

It's important to note that this finding emerged in statistical models where chronological age and the presence of chronic health conditions were also included. In other words, over and above the biological effects of aging, there's an independent effect of subjective age.

Feeling Younger Than Your Age Is Linked to Greater Life Satisfaction

People who feel younger than their actual age aren't just happier in the bedroom. In fact, they're living more satisfying lives in general. A separate longitudinal study out of England, based on a survey of more than 7,000 adults ages 50 and older, found that those who had a younger subjective age were the most content with their overall lives.

Specifically, those who felt like they were 25 to 30 years younger than they actually were reported the highest levels of life satisfaction. For example, people in their 90s who felt like they were still in their 60s were happier with their lives than people who felt closer to (or older than) their actual age.

Takeaways

These results are important because they tell us that if we want to understand sexual well-being among older adults, we need to look at more than just biology. We also need to consider psychological factors such as subjective age.

Independent of overall health status, people who feel older than they are seem to experience the sharpest declines in the quality of their sex lives. At the same time, the younger people feel, the more likely they are to maintain high satisfaction as they age, both in and out of the bedroom.

Broadly speaking, these findings remind us that aging is not just a biological process; it's also a psychological one. The age you feel may influence your sexual well-being and how you move through the world in ways that your chronological age alone can't explain. In short, our mindset around aging may be one of the most important factors in maintaining a satisfying sex life over time.

item.title: Psychopathy and Schizoid Personality Disorder: The Fear Divide
item.description:
Fear

Psychopathy and Schizoid Personality Disorder: The Fear Divide

The role of interpersonal anxiety in diagnosing personality disorders.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • One way to tell psychopathy and schizoid personality disorder apart is to look for evidence of fear.
  • Psychopaths feel less fear than normal because their amygdala is about 18 percent smaller than average.
  • People with schizoid PD feel more interpersonal fear than normal, which is why they often isolate themselves.

Some people assume that psychopaths and people with schizoid personality disorder must be similar because they both are emotionally hard to read. Making the distinction even more difficult, the media often prints sensationalized articles about antisocial loners who turn out to be serial killers. This leads some uninformed people to assume psychopaths and people described as schizoid must be connected or similar. However, if you compare the average psychopath with the average person with schizoid personality disorder (SPD) and look at their actual levels of fear, it is easy to tell them apart.

Note: I am using the terms psychopath and schizoid and SPD as shorthand terms for people who qualify for a full diagnosis of primary psychopathy or schizoid personality disorder. In this post, I am speaking only about psychopathy, not sociopathy or antisocial behavior disorder.

Some Brief Definitions

Psychopaths: While more research is needed, many experts believe that psychopaths are born with a smaller-than-normal amygdala and other brain abnormalities. They appear to be temperamentally predisposed to many of the following characteristics (Patrick, 2019):

  • Amoral
  • Low fear
  • Low empathy
  • Less emotional than normal
  • Low on desire for attachment
  • High on the need for stimulation
  • Restless and easily bored
  • Unconcerned about breaking rules or laws
  • Manipulative and deceitful
  • Very self-centered

Schizoids: They may have inherited some traits that predisposed them to develop SPD if mistreated, but they were not born with it and would not have developed it unless they experienced some of the following (Klein, 1995):

  • A severe lack of attunement by their caregivers
  • Abuse and/or neglect from infancy on
  • Very intrusive parenting

People with schizoid personality disorder tend to:

  • Mistrust other people
  • Hide their real feelings
  • Present a false self that appears more comfortable than they actually are
  • Have a very rich internal fantasy life that substitutes for relationships with actual people
  • Not know how to negotiate interpersonal differences
  • Fear attaching to people
  • Believe that whoever has the most power calls all the shots, and that the other person must obey or leave
  • Live alone and avoid intimate relationships to maintain control over their life

More detailed information on SPD is available in Ralph Klein’s excellent seven chapters in Disorders of the Self: The Masterson Approach (1995) and in chapters 3 and 13 of my book, Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations: The Pursuit of Love, Admiration, and Safety (2016).

Psychopaths and Fear

Psychopaths appear to be born rather than made. Research shows that their amygdala is, on average, 18 percent smaller than normal. Psychopathy can run in families, but their siblings can be perfectly normal. That is one of the puzzling things about psychopathy.

The Role of the Amygdala

The amygdala can be thought of as a stoplight that goes off when we are doing, or are about to do, something dangerous. It creates fear in us, so we stop. That fear keeps us alive and mostly out of trouble. It also helps us learn from our mistakes because fear is a very memorable emotion.

But, because psychopaths have a smaller-than-normal amygdala, they may feel a smaller-than-normal amount of fear. Even if they get hurt, the event is unlikely to become memorable enough to have a deterring impact on their future behavior.

Therefore, you can rule out psychopathy if the person complains about anxiety or authentically expresses fear in your presence.

Schizoids and Fear

People with SPD are believed to be born with a normal amygdala. We know that they can easily feel fear. Most schizoid defenses—the rich fantasy life, avoiding intimate relationships, being fiercely independent—are designed to protect them from their interpersonal fears.

Although there are inherited factors that can predispose someone to become schizoid, they are unlikely to develop a personality disorder if they have good parenting. Most SPD appears to be an adaptation to very difficult childhood circumstances. My schizoid clients report suffering some combination of early and continued abuse, neglect, or intrusiveness (Klein, Developmental Theory, 1995).

Examples of Neglect, Intrusiveness, and Abuse

  • Jane was sent to school in dirty clothing and basically ignored, while her siblings were given appropriate care and attention.
  • Ron’s mother often walked in when he was using the toilet or showering. When he complained, she replied: I saw everything you have when I changed your diapers. What are you making a fuss about?
  • Tina slept with a knife because her stepfather used to crawl into her bed when her mother kicked him out of their room during a fight. She was afraid that he would molest her if she fell asleep. Sometimes she would have to push his arm or leg off her during the night.
  • Tom was regularly beaten by his father for minor transgressions. His mother told him he was unwanted and worthless.

Schizoids Dissociate

My schizoid clients learned to dissociate as a response to their interpersonal fears. They could not physically leave the situation when they were being mistreated, so they learned to withdraw their awareness from their body and live in their mind. After a while, it became habitual, and they automatically dissociated whenever they felt afraid of other people.

Psychopaths Do Not Dissociate

Psychopaths do not need to dissociate to manage interpersonal fear because they do not usually experience it. Their main negative emotions around other people are boredom or disinterest.

Examples of Dissociation

Janie’s Glass Wall: Every time Janie met a man she liked, her emotions turned off, and she felt like a glass wall went down between them. She often went to work in a dissociated state and was surprised that other people could not tell. Janie had a dream that captured how she felt: I am a perfectly made-up face with carefully groomed hair. I am a head without a body, but nobody seems to notice. I bounce down the subway steps and onto a train (Greenberg, 2016).

Barton’s Mirror: Barton was in such a deep dissociated state when I first met him that he could not recognize his own face in the mirror. He tried to undo his dissociation by looking at his reflection and telling himself, “These are my eyes. This is my nose and mouth.”

Summary

Psychopaths experience diminished fear and less emotional stress than normal. That is why they appear comfortable in situations where ordinary people would feel afraid. People with schizoid personality disorders are the opposite. They cannot handle the amount of interpersonal fear they feel. The easiest way to tell the difference is that if the person displays real fear or anxiety, the person is highly unlikely to be a psychopath.

item.title: Listening to the Father Within
item.description:
Parenting

Listening to the Father Within

The hidden emotions that shape our parenting.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • The strongest, and sometimes most regrettable, parenting reactions reflect more than the present moment.
  • Understanding their hidden fears and hopes helps fathers respond with greater wisdom and emotional freedom.
  • Rather than asking, "What's wrong with me?" fathers can begin asking, "What was happening inside me?"
Source: Siegella/Pixabay

As I wrote in my previous post, men tend to have a harder time experiencing and coming to terms with regret than women do, based on gender socialization.

Nevertheless, in my work with fathers over the years, I have been able to develop a series of exercises designed to help them to contemplate and make sense of their regrets, rather than defend against them. This, in turn, can help them to grow, heal, and feel a renewed sense of hope and purpose as a dad, even when day-to-day parenthood has come to its conclusion.

In this post and subsequent ones, I will share some of those exercises, and some examples of how fathers have used them to their psychological advantage.

What Was Happening Inside of Me?

Choose a parenting moment that you regret, but instead of condemning yourself or blaming yourself, spend some time thinking about the following questions:

  1. What was I feeling in that moment?
  2. Who or what was I afraid of?
  3. Who or what was I trying to protect or rescue?
  4. What was I hoping to accomplish by acting/sounding the way I did?
  5. Did my regrettable response help, in any way at all, to accomplish that?
  6. In what ways did this evoke memories of my own childhood or adolescence?
  7. Whose voice was I using—my own, or someone else’s, perhaps someone from my childhood?
  8. How would I have preferred to handle the situation? What do I wish I had done differently?

Dennis, a 62-year-old father, met with me a few months after his oldest son, Luke, had left home for college. While he was proud of Luke, he found himself ruminating about a particularly difficult patch in their relationship during the winter of Luke’s junior year of high school.

At that time, Dennis and his wife received a call from the assistant principal that Dennis was selling the Adderall pills that had been prescribed for his ADHD, and would be suspended from school for a week. Not only were they upset that he had become involved in illegal drug-dealing, they were angry that he was not taking his medication.

When Luke returned from school, Dennis erupted at him, calling him terrible names, grounding him “forever,” grabbing Luke’s wallet and confiscating his new driver’s license, and ignoring him for days afterward.

“I can’t believe some of the things I said to him. I called him a loser, I called him a criminal, I told him he should be locked away. I told him he had embarrassed the entire family, and that he had ruined his younger brother’s reputation as well. I completely lost it with him. And then I wouldn’t talk to him for a week. Talk to him? I couldn’t even look at him! It was a horrible time…”

Gradually, Dennis told me, things began to improve, and in an overall sense, tension diminished. Dennis and Luke’s relationship slowly thawed, Dennis and his wife monitored Luke’s medication more carefully to ensure that he was taking it as prescribed, not distributing it, Luke’s baseball season started up, and the school year ended on a decent note.

Luke’s senior year also went relatively smoothly and Dennis and his wife were pleased that he was admitted to one of the colleges he wanted to attend. While he graduated with a lower GPA than they would have liked, at least there were no further legal or disciplinary issues.

Nevertheless, Dennis was not feeling pride in himself and the family for having successfully flown through this turbulence. In a way, this crisis had essentially been “buried alive,” with little subsequent discussion or exploration.

So it was not surprising that Dennis, more than a year later, was still finding himself consumed by self-hatred for his volcanic reaction and the hurtful things he had said to Luke, as nothing had ever been worked through.

With this in mind, we began working through the questions I supplied above:

  1. What was I feeling in that moment?

“Well, all I can remember feeling is pure, hot rage, just seeing red. It was anger, anger, anger, that was all…”

  1. Who or what was I afraid of?

“That’s a good question. I guess I was afraid of what was happening to Luke. How could my son be a drug dealer? What was to become of him? Was he going to go to jail? Would he ever graduate?”

  1. Who or what was I trying to protect or rescue?

“I suppose I was trying to protect Luke. From getting into further trouble. From digging a hole for himself. From ruining his future.”

  1. What was I hoping to accomplish by acting/sounding the way I did?

“I guess I’d answer that the same way: I was trying to get Luke to change his ways, to think about his actions, to not do stupid things. To ‘scare him straight’ as they say.”

  1. Did my regrettable response help, in any way at all, to accomplish that?

“I really don’t know. I still feel so awful about it. On the other hand, things did begin to settle down after my blow-up and there weren’t any subsequent transgressions. But all I can remember is the awful look on Luke’s face when I was ranting at him. He looked crushed.”

  1. In what ways did this evoke memories of my own childhood or adolescence?

“Oh, absolutely. My younger brother, Will, got into all kinds of trouble when he was a teenager, and it took him quite a while to grow out of it. He was a mess for quite some time, didn’t even start college until he was well into his 20s, and even then it took him like 8 years to finally finish. Now that I’m thinking about it, there really are some similarities there between Luke and my brother.”

  1. Whose voice was I using—my own, or someone else’s, perhaps someone from my childhood?

“Well, it was certainly my own voice, that’s for sure. I can still hear myself yelling. But my father was always screaming at Will when Will was in trouble, so it’s possible that I was channeling his voice, as well.”

  1. How would I have preferred to handle the situation? What do I wish I had done differently?

“One obvious thing is that I never asked him why he was doing what he was doing. I was just so angry that I wasn’t even curious. I still don’t know what was going on for him, but I wish I had taken the time to ask.”

In the next post, I will discuss the ways in which Dennis’s self-examination placed him on a pathway toward greater empathy—and improvements in the father-son relationship.

item.title: The Universal Importance of Self-Motivation and Personal Discipline
item.description:
Motivation

The Universal Importance of Self-Motivation and Personal Discipline

Our greatest strength advances by aligning merit with universal principles.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Universal truths are, self-evidently, nonnegotiable.
  • History informs that the constant pursuit of universal truths has advanced merit and achievements.
  • Universal laws were not invented; they were discovered through systematic engagement with reality.
Source: jplenio / Pixabay

Our greatest strength in advancing meritorious universal skills and knowledge has always been the unwavering application of the ever-present dawn of self-motivation and personal discipline, together with the practical, physical, and intellectual adherence to the immutable principles revealed through the precise, effortful application of critical thinking, higher-order reasoning, and a systematic search for objective, applied universal truths.

This disciplined pursuit is also reflected in Responsibility Theory, which holds that the individual is responsible for and has power over what they think, do, say, learn, and choose, and understands that choices have consequences.

Throughout history, this competence-based, meritorious process, along with the constant pursuit of universal truths and excellence, has led to the discovery and application of these universal laws—all of which have then continued to advance and further enhance the capacities of merit, achievements, competence, and standards of excellence (Aiston & Fitzgerald, 2024; Bandura, 2006; Chen, 2026; Kant, 1785/1996; Holmquist et al., 2014; Lombardi, 2023; Popper, 2005; Prašević, 2024; Purje, 2014; Sabic‑El‑Rayess, 2016).

Significance of Universal Laws

These universal truths, which are—self-evidently—nonnegotiable, have come to be known as the laws of physics, energy, motion, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, mathematics, and the universal biological processes that govern human development, consciousness, and life itself (Asimov, 1993; Baars & Edelman, 2012; Belot, 1998; McInerny et al., 2025; Natali & Leyh, 2025; Nurjanah et al., 2025; Palmgren et al., 2025; Sanfey, 2023; Vanchurin et al., 2022).

Source: Loaivat / Pixabay

As the human brain, body, and consciousness developed, so did the capacity to think at a deeper level, analyze, and move toward even more sophisticated levels of critical thinking and higher-order reasoned evaluation. All of this helped to augment deeper understandings of the self and the world (Aumann, 2024; Crick & Koch, 1998; Frith, 2021; Georgiev, 2023; León & Zahavi, 2023).

Contemporary neuroscience research also shows that the development of consciousness enabled humans to reflect, compare, contrast, and incessantly question, judge, and test observations and empirical experiences against self-reflective thoughts, the opinions of others, and the associated reality of the external world (Aumann, 2024; Crick & Koch, 1998; Elgavi & Hamo, 2025; Frith, 2021; Georgiev, 2023; Kuhn, 2026; León & Zahavi, 2023; Natali & Leyh, 2025).

A considered and profound example of this process of analyzing the external world and the associated process of self-analysis occurred in 1637, when René Descartes declared in French: “Je pense, donc je suis,” which was eventually translated into Latin (Cogito, ergo sum) in 1644 in his book Principia Philosophiae (Principles of Philosophy).

This was ultimately translated into English—“I think, therefore I am”—in 1649, in the book: A Discourse of Method for the Well Guiding of Reason, and the Seeking in of Truth in the Sciences (Gijn, 2005; Haas, 1992; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2026).

Importantly and self-evidently, none of these universal laws were invented; they were discovered through constant self-reflection, unrelenting internal and external questioning of self and the world, plus the ongoing process of systematic scientific method of engagement with reality that included trial and error, along with the uncompromising cumulative questioning and refinement of skills, intellectual curiosity, and inquiry (Basar & Batur, 2025; Popper, 2005; Kant, 1785/1996; Kaya et al., 2025; McPhee & Cox, 2025).

History and research affirm that this process of constant systematic questioning and ongoing analysis, along with deeper levels of investigation and the application of the scientific method of research, higher-order reasoning, and incessant inquiry-based exploration, have been the cognitive and skill-based mechanisms through which individuals begin to recognize and apply the universal principles that distinguish immutable truths from opinions (Kaya et al., 2025; McPhee & Cox, 2025).

The scientific method of research further informs and demonstrates that understanding universal principles is irrefutably essential for individual and social advancement in terms of intellect, skills, knowledge, and associated technological development, for informed, ongoing, beneficial, objective decision-making to take place.

All these principles and practices develop, advance, and enhance merit, achievements, competence, and standards of excellence (Basar & Batur, 2025; Glaesser, 2019; McPhee & Cox, 2025; Ropohl et al., 2017; Sabic-El-Rayess, 2016; Vitello et al., 2021; Xie & Yusuf, 2026).

Universal Laws Across Disciplines

These universal principles and laws apply to every discipline one cares to mention. As history shows, individuals and societies thrive when they recognize and apply these principles. There are numerous examples of this in engineering, medicine, the sciences, sports, and the arts, and of course, much, much more. The evidence is irrefutable: To ignore universal laws is, to say the least, fraught with immense concerns. Universal truths do not negotiate.

The immutable, nonnegotiable laws governing structural integrity; biological function; cognitive, intellectual, and skill development; and the universal truth of mathematical reasoning do not change because of opinions.

For example, there was a time when the Earth was considered to be flat. Although this opinion, belief, and social convention did shape thinking and action for a brief period in history, this social convention did not alter reality (Afnan et al., 2025; Brízová et al., 2018; Elgavi & Hamo, 2025; Monaghan et al., 2026; Navarro-Quiroz et al., 2026).

Source: u_ozhkrzut0x/Pixabay

Always and Forever

Self-evidently and immutably, universal laws do not vary. History and objective empirical evidence are unequivocal and immutably nonnegotiable: Humanity advances and has advanced when universal principles are recognized and applied (Asimov, 1993; Belot, 1998; Crick & Koch, 1998; Hill, 2025; Lopes, 2009; Palmgren et al., 2025; Vanchurin et al., 2022; Vieland, 2015).

Therefore, irrefutably, our greatest strength—from a forever and universal perspective in terms of achievements—has always been the rational, reasoned, and enlightened adherence to the immutable universal principles of merit, achievement, competence, and the pursuit of excellence (Aiston & Fitzgerald, 2024; Goode, 2026; Ka Yuk Chan & Chen, 2024; Terzi, 2020).

item.title: The Only Mindset That Can Guarantee a Happy Life
item.description:
Happiness

The Only Mindset That Can Guarantee a Happy Life

Happy people don't just rely on optimism. They have another trick up their sleeve.

Posted July 23, 2026

Source: Maurício Mascaro / Pexels

Most happiness advice rests on a simple assumption: that the goal is to feel better, and that the path there runs through thinking more positively, reframing the setback or hunting for the silver lining.

But a substantial body of research on emotion suggests something stranger and, in its own way, more freeing. The mindset most consistently linked to well-being has very little to do with generating good feelings and much more to do with how a person relates to the feelings that aren't good at all.

Psychologists who study emotion regulation have found, again and again, that the people who cope best with difficulty are not the ones who experience fewer negative emotions. They are the ones who have learned to accept those emotions when they arrive, rather than fighting to push them away.

Researchers in this area, including psychologist Iris Mauss and her collaborators, describe this disposition as emotional acceptance: meeting anger, sadness or anxiety with a kind of curiosity and nonjudgment, instead of treating each feeling as proof that something has gone wrong.

Why Happiness Comes Last to Those Trying Hardest to Find It

What makes this finding counterintuitive is the direction it runs: People who practice this kind of acceptance tend to report better psychological health over time, including fewer negative emotions overall, than people who work hard to suppress or talk themselves out of how they feel, a pattern borne out in a 2018 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology that followed participants through laboratory and six-month longitudinal designs.

The underlying mechanism becomes easier to understand once it’s laid out plainly. Judging an emotion tends to add a second layer of discomfort on top of the first. Feeling anxious is, on its own, an uncomfortable enough experience; feeling anxious and then becoming frustrated with oneself for being anxious tends to be considerably worse, and it’s usually this second layer, rather than the original feeling, that spirals into something harder to manage.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, the clinical framework built around this idea, gives a name to the opposite habit: experiential avoidance, the reflexive effort to escape or suppress unwanted internal experiences. Decades of clinical research connect experiential avoidance to higher, not lower, rates of anxiety and depression, including a 2022 meta-analysis published in the Journal of Contextual Behavioral Science that pooled findings from more than 400 studies and over 135,000 participants and suggested that the resistance itself is often what fuels the distress.

This research reframes a piece of conventional wisdom that sounds harmless on its surface but tends to function differently in practice: the instinct to remain relentlessly upbeat, regardless of circumstance.

Forcing positivity onto a genuinely difficult moment rarely neutralizes the underlying feeling; more often, it simply adds a layer of shame once the positivity fails to take hold. People who feel obligated to be happy, according to a 2011 study published in the journal Emotion, are more likely to report distress when they inevitably fall short of that standard than people who never set the bar so high to begin with.

article continues after advertisement

The mindset that seems to guarantee well-being, then, is not optimism so much as permission — the acknowledgment that a feeling is allowed to exist without first justifying itself.

Happiness Is Not a Fixed State

Where this picture becomes more interesting, and more honest, is in research on what’s known as emodiversity, a term coined by psychologist Jordi Quoidbach to describe the variety of emotions a person experiences, rather than simply their ratio of good to bad. His work, laid out in a 2014 study published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, suggests that people with a richer emotional palette — who move through a wide range of states, including the uncomfortable ones, instead of cycling between forced cheer and flat numbness — tend to report better outcomes across both mental and physical health.

The implied goal isn’t a life free of bad days but one with a fuller instrument panel, in which sadness, boredom and irritation are allowed to register rather than being smoothed over before they can be understood.

This nuance matters because acceptance can easily be oversimplified into passivity. Accepting an emotion is not the same as accepting a bad situation; frustration at a toxic job, for instance, is useful information rather than something to simply sit with indefinitely. The mindset in discussion here is not resignation but patience—letting a feeling exist long enough to learn what it’s pointing toward, instead of treating its presence as something to fight on principle.

Psychologists working in this space are still refining where exactly healthy acceptance gives way to harmful complacency, and that ongoing debate is part of what makes the research feel credible rather than overly tidy.

Happiness in Practice

In everyday terms, this mindset tends to show up as a small but consistent habit: naming a feeling instead of immediately trying to manage it away. It looks like noticing, simply, “This is disappointment,” rather than reaching at once for a reason to feel otherwise. It also tends to ease the pressure on good days, since there’s less compulsion to perform contentment for an audience, whether that audience is other people or simply the more critical voice inside one’s own head.

None of this amounts to a promise of a life without difficulty. What the research does suggest, fairly consistently, is that the people who stop treating difficulty as a malfunction tend to arrive at a sturdier, more durable form of well-being than those still chasing an uninterrupted good mood.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: Coping With Life’s Challenges Using True Optimism
item.description:
Optimism

Coping With Life’s Challenges Using True Optimism

Why optimism is more than positive thinking.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • True optimism involves more than positive thinking or good intentions.
  • Our mindset will determine whether we will be able to cope with what life throws at us.
  • When we become prisoners of our thoughts, we think we are powerless to change ourselves or our circumstances.
  • Knowing you have the ultimate freedom to choose your attitude is important when coping with life’s challenges.
Source: Patpitchaya/Shutterstock

We are living in uncertain and dangerous times. Globally, we face many formidable challenges in the political, social, cultural, and economic systems upon which our societies depend. On the individual level, our most basic human needs, such as security, community, self-esteem, and achievement, are also being challenged.

We are also facing rapid changes that pressure our ability to cope. Fundamentally, it is our mindset that will determine whether or not we will cope with and, hopefully, thrive in these new circumstances.

The world-renowned psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor Viktor E. Frankl is perhaps best known for practicing and espousing “freedom of will” in terms of choosing an attitude when experiencing unavoidable or inescapable suffering.1

Let’s face it, human beings are, by nature, creatures of habit. Searching for a life that is predictable and within our comfort zone, we rely on routine and learned thinking patterns. We create pathways in our minds in much the same way that a path is beaten through a grass field from repeated use.

Because these patterns are automatic, we may believe that these habitual ways of thinking and behaving are both necessary and beyond our control. Thus, we rationalize our responses to life and fall prey to forces that limit our potential as human beings.

By viewing ourselves as relatively powerless, driven by instinct and outside forces, the possibility that we create, or at least co-create, our own reality becomes difficult to grasp. Instead, we often lock ourselves inside our own mental prisons. We lose sight of our own natural potential and that of others. In essence, we become “prisoners of our thoughts.”2

However, in line with Frankl’s teachings, no matter how desperate our situation in life may appear or be, we always have the ultimate freedom to choose our attitude. This responsibility is personal and cannot be transferred to someone else. It can be viewed, moreover, as both the foundation of and the driver behind our ability to cope with and respond to whatever challenges in life, including societal changes, come our way.

Frankl relied upon an overarching belief system, or mindset, about coping, which he called his coping maxim, to help him sustain an optimistic and passionate view about his own chances of survival in the Nazi concentration camps. His extraordinary story of finding meaning amid the horrors of his imprisonment vividly showed that we don’t have to be prisoners of our thoughts and that we can exercise what he called the “last of the human freedoms,” the ultimate freedom to choose one’s attitude in response to whatever life circumstances we face.

We all struggle with situations in life that are beyond our control. Whether these situations involve the personal and collective challenges from an unexpected shift in the political landscape due to an election or from any other changes that disrupt our life in some way, we can still find and learn that life doesn’t just happen to us; we happen to life and we make it meaningful. And it is by changing our mindset, beginning proactively with our choice of attitude, that we can respond to life, as Frankl famously espoused, by being responsible.

As we venture through life, we encounter both joyful and sorrowful times. Although we might wish to experience only the happy times, we know that to live a full life, we must be prepared to experience challenging and often painful situations. Life is about opposites: day and night, sickness and health, good and evil, wealth and poverty, and so on. Opposites are beneficial because they help us define and contrast things; we need to know one to know the other.3

Importantly, it is in the wholeness of life that we build our resilience and coping abilities to face all of life’s challenges. It is in the wholeness of life that we experience the most meaning.

Building our capacity to cope depends upon and significantly benefits from our choice of attitude. In this regard, it is important to underscore that when we choose an optimistic attitude, or what can be called “true optimism,” we make three choices:

  1. Choose a positive attitude toward the situation at hand
  2. Choose an attitude that supports a form of creative visualization about what is possible
  3. Choose an attitude that generates passion for the action needed to make the possible become a reality

In other words, being a “true optimist” requires more than just positive thinking. Positive affirmations, like good intentions, aren’t enough in and of themselves. We need to be able to visualize the possibilities that may or can result from our choice of attitude and, moreover, be able to feel the emotion and passion behind our choice of attitude that will help us actualize or realize such possibilities.

In the final analysis, although we may not be totally free from the various conditions or situations that confront us in both our personal and work lives, the important thing is that we can choose how we respond, at the very least through our choice of attitude. The keys to freedom from life’s prison cells—real and imagined—are within, and within reach.

So how about you? Are you ready to escape the inner mental prison that may be holding you back from achieving your full potential? Will you choose an optimistic attitude to cope with whatever life throws at you? Are you a “true optimist?”

item.title: Are the Kids Alright? Teens' Usage of AI Companions Is Up
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Are the Kids Alright? Teens' Usage of AI Companions Is Up

Why people seek AI support and romance and how this might affect them long-term.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Research is finding that teens are using AI chatbots as romantic partners and/or emotional supports.
  • One in five adolescents report forming emotional or romantic bonds with AI companions.
  • Overreliance on nonhuman interactions can stunt development of empathy, boundaries, and conflict management.

Recent studies speak to a trend: Teens are using artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots as romantic partners and/or emotional supports (Ha and colleagues, 2026). Research finds that up to one in five adolescents report forming emotional or romantic bonds with AI companions. For example, a study published in the Journal of Adolescence found that 60 percent of U.S. teens have used AI chatbots, with more than 11 percent using them daily.

A study conducted by Male Allies UK highlighted that roughly 20 percent of boys aged 12 to 16 know a peer “dating” an AI chatbot, and more than a quarter prefer AI companionship over real-life relationships. Further, the Center for Democracy and Technology (CDT) noted that one in five high schoolers report a personal or romantic relationship with AI, and 42 percent use AI for companionship or to support mental well-being. Why choose AI companions?

Source: Andres Siimon / Unsplash

There’s nothing like constant validation

Chatbots offer nonjudgmental, consistent validation and are programmed to agree. On the downside, however, a lack of genuine, reciprocal engagement can stunt social-skill development, and teens may bypass the uncomfortable but important work of human conflict resolution. Not learning these social skills can increase long-term vulnerability to loneliness and anxiety.

Overcoming the hurdle of social anxiety

Many teens find AI interactions less stressful than real-life social situations, allowing them to bypass awkwardness and fear of rejection. The struggle is real, and it is easier, more convenient, and sometimes more comfortable to talk to AI via a screen than a flesh-and-blood human. If someone is lonely and does not have many friends, a chatbot is there in a pinch by simply typing.

Support for mental health concerns

Many persons struggle with loneliness, anxiety, or depression. AI chatbots, when prompted, dispense mental health advice of varying veracity and quality that users can take to heart and follow without asking a second opinion. AI companions are designed to be sycophantic and agreeable so that more and more people will use them more often. So AI often generates a response users want to hear: “Break up with her,” “Quit your job,” etc. Further, the use of chatbots for counsel and counseling is often kept in secret from parents, friends, and even the human therapists they may see, meaning that helping professionals nowadays should inquire about AI chatbot use as a matter of course.

Why AI companionship can become problematic

Social offloading is an overreliance on nonhuman interactions and companionship; it’s also referred to as "relational displacement,” where people substitute AI interactions for human relationships. Why might this be a problem? It can lead to a stunting of conflict resolution skills, emotional resilience (and patience), and empathy. This is to say that when people grow to depend on chatbots for validation, they can opt out of learning experiences that stem from everyday disagreements and handling conflicting points of view with others. They don’t have to persevere with others or deepen their understanding of the human need for reciprocity (e.g., You get what you give; It's good to listen, not just talk), nor do they have to learn about personal boundaries (e.g., not asking inappropriate questions, say, at 3 a.m., by text).

AI sycophancy can alter users’ expectations about how and when friends, family, or a real, live partner will respond to them. When on-demand, immediate support with other humans is not instantly gratified, users can become frustrated, and this can heighten long-term vulnerability to withdrawal, isolation, depression, and anxiety. All this to say, some of the kids (and adults) are not alright, and AI may or may not be the answer to their questions and challenges.
